quiz.q: What is the approximate current value of the Hubble constant?
o: About 70 km/s per megaparsec
About 300,000 km/s per megaparsec
About 3 km/s per megaparsec
About 700,000 km/s per megaparsec
quiz.e: The Hubble constant is measured at roughly 70 km/s per megaparsec, relating distance to recession velocity.

quiz.q: Approximately how far is the Sun from the galactic center?
o: About 26,000 light-years
About 4 light-years
About 100,000 light-years
About 1 light-year
quiz.e: The Sun lies in the Orion Arm, roughly 26,000 light-years from the Milky Way's center.

quiz.q: What are two leading dark matter particle candidates?
o: WIMPs and axions
Photons and neutrinos
Protons and electrons
Quasars and pulsars
quiz.e: WIMPs (weakly interacting massive particles) and axions are leading hypothesized dark matter particles.

quiz.q: What does the cosmological constant represent in one leading dark energy hypothesis?
o: The combined gravitational pull of all matter
A repulsive force from dark matter particles
An energy inherent to empty space itself
The leftover heat from the Big Bang
quiz.e: The cosmological constant treats dark energy as an intrinsic property of space itself, as allowed by Einstein's equations.

quiz.q: What did the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics recognize?
o: The discovery of gravitational waves from merging black holes
The discovery of the accelerating expansion of the universe
The discovery of dark matter through galaxy rotation curves
The detection of the Higgs boson at the Large Hadron Collider
quiz.e: The 2011 Nobel Prize honored the discovery, via distant supernovae, that the universe's expansion is accelerating.

quiz.q: What kind of stars dominate elliptical galaxies?
o: Young, blue stars, with intense ongoing star formation
A mix of newly born stars forming in spiral arms
Mainly neutron stars, with no normal stars left
Older stars, with little ongoing star formation
quiz.e: Elliptical galaxies are dominated by older stellar populations and have little gas for new star formation.

quiz.q: About how many stars does the Milky Way contain?
o: 100 to 400 billion
About 1 million
About 8
About 88
quiz.e: The Milky Way is estimated to contain 100-400 billion stars.

quiz.q: What surrounds the Milky Way's disk and contains old globular clusters and dark matter?
o: The galactic halo
The galactic bar
The event horizon
The photosphere
quiz.e: The halo surrounding the Milky Way's disk contains old globular clusters along with much of the galaxy's dark matter.

quiz.q: Why does Hubble's Law imply the universe has no center of expansion?
o: Because the Milky Way sits at the center and all other galaxies move away from it
Because galaxies farther away recede more slowly, so distant regions are nearly stationary
Because the expansion began at a single point in space that we can no longer observe
Because every point in space sees all others receding proportionally to distance
quiz.e: Since recession velocity scales with distance from any vantage point, no single location can be identified as the center.

quiz.q: What best describes gravitational lensing as evidence for dark matter?
o: Massive clusters make background galaxies look brighter and bluer, revealing hot gas in the foreground
Dark matter particles absorb background light, leaving dark patches that map where the unseen mass lies
Massive objects bend light from background galaxies in ways that reveal unseen mass
Light from background galaxies is redshifted by the cluster's motion, revealing how fast the dark matter spins
quiz.e: Gravitational lensing shows how mass (including invisible dark matter) bends and distorts light from more distant sources.

quiz.q: Which era does the CMB give astronomers a snapshot of?
o: The universe about 380,000 years after the Big Bang
The present-day universe
The very first fraction of a second after the Big Bang
The formation of the solar system
quiz.e: The CMB was released when the universe became transparent to light, about 380,000 years after the Big Bang.

quiz.q: What do tiny temperature fluctuations in the CMB reveal?
o: The seeds of structure that grew into galaxies and galaxy clusters
The first stars that ignited and reionized the universe
The pattern of stars that later formed the Milky Way's spiral arms
The density of dark energy in each region of space
quiz.e: Small CMB temperature variations mark the density fluctuations that later grew into cosmic structure.

o: About 68%
About 5%
About 27%
About 100%
quiz.e: Dark energy makes up roughly 68% of the universe's total mass-energy content, the dominant component.

Elliptical galaxies
Barred spiral galaxies
Lenticular galaxies

o: Ordinary matter interacts with light and makes up about 5% of the universe
Ordinary matter emits no light and makes up about 27% of the universe
Ordinary matter interacts with light and makes up about 68% of the universe
Ordinary matter is invisible to telescopes and makes up about 95% of the universe
quiz.e: Baryonic (ordinary) matter, which interacts with light, is only about 5% of the universe's total mass-energy.

It clumps into halos around galaxies due to gravity
It collects inside stars, increasing their core temperatures
It collapses into thin, dense disks within galaxies

quiz.q: What does the term 'standard candle' refer to in cosmology?

An object of known size used to measure cosmic distances, such as a distant galaxy cluster
A source of known redshift used to calibrate telescope instruments, such as a quasar's spectrum
A star whose spectrum is used to calibrate the temperature scale, such as a main-sequence star

A thin line of young blue stars along one arm, from which star formation spreads
A dense spherical halo of stars around the nucleus, from which the arms wind outward
A straight bar of stars through the center from which spiral arms emerge
quiz.e: Barred spirals have a central bar structure from which the spiral arms extend, unlike ordinary spirals.

quiz.q: Why is the discovery of the accelerating universe considered surprising?

Scientists expected the expansion to continue at a constant speed forever
Scientists expected distant supernovae to look brighter than nearby ones
Scientists expected the expansion to have stopped by now and reversed

The creation of NASA by Congress in 1958

A larger Titan rocket that carried enough fuel to reach each planet

A return of the probe to Earth orbit so its samples could be recovered
A deliberate plunge into Saturn's atmosphere to end the mission safely
A deliberate landing on Enceladus to test whether its geysers hide life

The first American space station, launched in 1973
The first reusable crewed spacecraft, launched in 1981

Improved balance, stronger immunity, and faster healing of wounds
Bone density loss, muscle atrophy, and fluid shifts
Skin thickening, increased appetite, and gradual loss of hearing

o: A crewed test flight of Orion on a Falcon Heavy rocket that orbited Earth in 2020
An uncrewed Orion capsule flight on a Delta IV rocket that circled Earth twice in 2014
An uncrewed lander test of Starship and the Space Launch System touching down on the Moon in 2022
An uncrewed test flight of Orion and the Space Launch System around the Moon in 2022

quiz.q: What distinguishes Apollo 13 as a celebrated mission despite failing to land on the Moon?
o: The crew conducted a spacewalk to repair the oxygen tank on the way back
The crew and mission control improvised a safe return after a near-disaster
A backup crew launched a rescue spacecraft that docked and brought the astronauts home
The crew replaced the heat shield in orbit, saving themselves from a reentry failure

quiz.q: What does the transit method measure to detect an exoplanet?
o: The periodic shift in a star's spectral lines as a planet's gravity tugs it back and forth
The tiny change in a star's position on the sky as a planet pulls it in a small circle
The periodic dimming of a star's light as a planet passes in front of it
The brief brightening of a background star's light as a planet's gravity bends it
quiz.e: The transit method detects planets via the small, periodic dimming of starlight as the planet crosses in front of its star.

quiz.q: What does the transit method primarily reveal about a planet?
o: Its mass, based on how deeply the star's light dips
Its distance from Earth, based on how much the star dims
Its size (radius), based on how much light it blocks
Its surface gravity, based on how long each transit lasts
quiz.e: The amount of starlight blocked during a transit reveals the planet's size relative to its star.

quiz.q: What orbital alignment is required for the transit method to work?
o: The planet's orbit must lie in the habitable zone of its star
The planet must be larger than its star to block enough light
The planet's orbit must be nearly edge-on as seen from Earth
The planet's orbit must be tilted about 45 degrees from our line of sight
quiz.e: Only planets whose orbits are aligned edge-on from our viewpoint will transit and be detectable this way.

quiz.q: Which NASA mission used the transit method to monitor over 150,000 stars simultaneously?
o: Kepler
Voyager
Cassini
Hubble
quiz.e: The Kepler space telescope, launched in 2009, monitored more than 150,000 stars using the transit method.

quiz.q: What does the radial velocity method detect?
o: The periodic dimming of starlight as a planet crosses in front of its star's disk
The tiny brightening of a background star as a planet's gravity acts as a lens
A star's small back-and-forth wobble caused by an orbiting planet's gravity
The infrared glow of a planet's warm atmosphere, separate from its star's light
quiz.e: Radial velocity detects the Doppler shift in a star's spectral lines caused by its gravitational wobble from an orbiting planet.

quiz.q: What does the radial velocity method primarily reveal about a planet?
o: Its exact radius and its orbital inclination
Its true mass and its atmospheric composition
A lower limit on its mass and its orbital period
Its density and the tilt of its rotation axis
quiz.e: Radial velocity reveals a planet's orbital period and a minimum mass, but not its size directly.

quiz.q: Which exoplanet was the first confirmed around a Sun-like star, discovered via radial velocity in 1995?
o: 51 Pegasi b
Kepler-452b
Proxima Centauri b
TRAPPIST-1b
quiz.e: 51 Pegasi b, discovered by Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz in 1995, was the first confirmed exoplanet around a Sun-like star.

quiz.q: Why did early radial velocity surveys tend to find 'hot Jupiters' first?
o: Hot Jupiters are by far the most common planets, so surveys encountered them first
Their bright atmospheres shine in infrared, making them easy to spot by direct imaging
Their strong magnetic fields disturb the star's spectrum, making the star easy to flag
Massive, close-orbiting planets cause a larger, easier-to-detect stellar wobble
quiz.e: Radial velocity is most sensitive to massive planets orbiting close to their star, which cause the largest stellar wobble.

quiz.q: Combining transit and radial velocity data allows astronomers to calculate what?
o: A planet's age, indicating whether it formed early or late
A planet's density, indicating whether it's rocky, gaseous, or icy
A planet's distance from Earth, indicating how bright its star appears
A planet's rotation period, indicating whether it is tidally locked
quiz.e: Radius (from transit) combined with mass (from radial velocity) yields density, revealing likely composition.

quiz.q: What is direct imaging of exoplanets generally limited to?
o: Small, old, cool planets close to their star
Large, young, hot planets far from their star
Large, hot planets close to their bright star
Planets that transit in front of their stars
quiz.e: Direct imaging requires blocking a star's glare, which is only feasible for large, hot planets orbiting far from bright stars.

quiz.q: What is gravitational microlensing able to detect that other methods cannot?
o: Planets orbiting very close to hot, bright stars
Planets that pass in front of their stars every few days
Free-floating 'rogue' planets not orbiting any star
Planets whose surfaces are covered in liquid oceans
quiz.e: Microlensing can detect distant or unbound rogue planets since it relies on gravitational light-bending, not starlight from the planet's system.

quiz.q: What is the habitable zone?
o: The range of distances where a planet's gravity is strong enough to hold an atmosphere around it
The region around a star where a planet's orbit is stable for billions of years without ejection
The region of a galaxy where heavy elements are abundant enough for rocky planets to form
The range of orbital distances where a planet could have liquid water on its surface
quiz.e: The habitable zone is the distance range from a star where surface temperatures could allow liquid water.

quiz.q: Why are Venus and Mars not considered habitable despite being near the Sun's habitable zone?
o: They orbit too close to the Sun, so their oceans have evaporated, and both lack any protective magnetic field
Their atmospheres are unsuitable: Venus is too thin to hold heat, while Mars has runaway greenhouse warming
Their atmospheres are unsuitable: Venus has runaway greenhouse warming, Mars has too thin an atmosphere
Their orbits are too eccentric: both swing so far from the Sun that surface water freezes yearly
quiz.e: Being in the habitable zone alone isn't enough; atmospheric conditions on Venus and Mars prevent stable liquid water.

quiz.q: What atmospheric gas is considered a strong candidate biosignature because it is chemically reactive and needs replenishment?
o: Oxygen
Nitrogen
Carbon dioxide
Hydrogen
quiz.e: Oxygen reacts readily and would disappear without ongoing biological production (like photosynthesis), making it a strong biosignature candidate.

quiz.q: Why is the coexistence of methane and oxygen considered a particularly strong biosignature?
o: Both gases come from volcanoes, so their coexistence suggests ongoing geological activity instead of life
The two gases are inert toward each other, so their coexistence suggests the planet is very old and stable
The two gases react with each other, so their coexistence suggests active ongoing production
Both gases are easily produced by sunlight splitting water, so their coexistence suggests a wet atmosphere
quiz.e: Since methane and oxygen react and would otherwise deplete each other, finding both suggests continuous replenishment, often by life.

quiz.q: What technique does JWST use to detect gases in a transiting exoplanet's atmosphere?
o: Transmission spectroscopy
Radial velocity
Direct photography
Radar imaging
quiz.e: Transmission spectroscopy analyzes starlight filtered through a planet's atmosphere during transit to identify its gases.

quiz.q: What is a key challenge in interpreting biosignature gases?
o: Their spectral signatures overlap with common gases like nitrogen, making them hard to separate
Some can also be produced by non-biological (abiotic) processes, creating false positives
They break down within hours in any atmosphere, so they are seen on newly formed planets
Most are produced by one species of microbe, so they apply to Earth-like life
quiz.e: Certain biosignature gases can form through geological or photochemical processes without life, requiring careful interpretation.

quiz.q: What does the TRAPPIST-1 system consist of?
o: Seven roughly Earth-sized planets orbiting a small red dwarf star
Three Jupiter-sized planets orbiting a pair of white dwarf stars
A single Neptune-sized planet orbiting a young blue giant star
Seven gas giants orbiting a Sun-like star every few hundred days
quiz.e: TRAPPIST-1 hosts seven roughly Earth-sized planets, several within the star's habitable zone, orbiting a red dwarf.

quiz.q: What does the Drake Equation estimate?
o: The number of exoplanets orbiting stars in the galaxy
The number of stars that will become supernovae each century
The number of communicating civilizations in the galaxy
The probability that a planet's atmosphere contains life
quiz.e: The Drake Equation is a probabilistic framework for estimating the number of communicating civilizations in the Milky Way.

quiz.q: As of the mid-2020s, roughly how many exoplanets have been confirmed?
o: More than 5,000
About 8
About 100
About 500,000
quiz.e: More than 5,000 exoplanets had been confirmed by the mid-2020s, spanning a huge diversity of types.

quiz.q: What planet types, common among exoplanets, have no equivalent in our solar system?
o: Super-Earths and mini-Neptunes
Gas giants and ice giants
Terrestrial planets and dwarf planets
Rogue planets and comets
quiz.e: Super-Earths and mini-Neptunes are common exoplanet categories that do not exist among our solar system's planets.

quiz.q: What challenge do tidally locked planets around red dwarf stars face for habitability?
o: Their orbits are so eccentric that their seasons swing wildly between scorching and freezing each year
Their rapid rotation produces violent winds that strip the atmosphere away within days
Their gravity is too weak to retain water, so any oceans escape into space
Extreme temperature differences between their permanent day and night sides
quiz.e: Tidally locked planets always show one side to their star, creating extreme temperature contrasts between hemispheres.

quiz.q: What is TESS?
o: A European Space Agency mission launched in 2009 that watches a single patch of sky for faint, distant transiting planets
A NASA mission launched in 2018 that surveys bright, nearby stars for transiting exoplanets across the whole sky
A NASA infrared space telescope launched in 2021 that studies the atmospheres of known exoplanets in detail
A ground-based survey begun in 2012 that measures radial velocity wobbles of nearby stars across the northern sky
quiz.e: TESS (Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite) continues Kepler's transit-detection work across the full sky.

quiz.q: What does astrometry measure to detect exoplanets?
o: A star's regular dimming as a planet passes in front of it
A star's small shift in spectral lines as the planet pulls it
A star's brief brightening as a planet bends light from behind
A star's tiny side-to-side positional wobble on the sky
quiz.e: Astrometry detects the small positional wobble in a star caused by an orbiting planet's gravity, viewed across the sky.

quiz.q: How does the habitable zone's location change with a star's properties?
o: Hotter, more luminous stars have farther and wider habitable zones
All stars have an identical habitable zone
Cooler stars have farther habitable zones than hotter stars
The habitable zone is unrelated to a star's luminosity
quiz.e: A star's habitable zone shifts outward and widens as its luminosity and temperature increase.

quiz.q: What raises concern about the habitability of Proxima Centauri b, despite being in its star's habitable zone?
o: Its host is an active red dwarf star, raising radiation exposure concerns
Its host star is about to become a red giant, so the planet will soon be engulfed
Its host star is dim and quiet, so too little radiation reaches it for liquid water
Its orbit is extremely eccentric, carrying it out of the habitable zone for most of each year
quiz.e: Proxima Centauri b orbits a flare-active red dwarf, raising questions about radiation exposure despite its habitable-zone location.

quiz.q: What factors, beyond distance from a star, are thought to support long-term habitability?
o: A thick hydrogen envelope, a very large mass, and a fast spin
Frequent giant impacts, intense volcanism, and a highly eccentric orbit
A tidally locked rotation, a very thin atmosphere, and heavy cratering
Plate tectonics, a protective magnetic field, and a stable orbit
quiz.e: Plate tectonics, a magnetic field shielding against stellar wind, and orbital stability are additional supporting factors for habitability.

quiz.q: What is Kepler-452b sometimes called, and why?
o: 'Earth's twin,' for being an Earth-sized rocky world with an atmosphere confirmed to match Earth's
A 'hot Jupiter,' for being a Jupiter-sized gas giant orbiting its star in just a few days
'Earth's cousin,' for being a near-Earth-sized planet in a Sun-like star's habitable zone
A 'rogue planet,' for being a free-floating world that travels through space without a host star
quiz.e: Kepler-452b is called 'Earth's cousin' for its near-Earth size and habitable-zone orbit around a Sun-like star, though its composition is unconfirmed.

quiz.q: Each exoplanet detection method has different biases. What does direct imaging favor?
o: Small planets close to their star
Planets that cross their star's disk
Large planets far from their star
Old, cool planets near their star
quiz.e: Direct imaging favors large, bright planets far enough from their star's glare to be resolved separately.

quiz.q: What advantage do multiple detection methods used together provide for a single exoplanet system?
o: Confirmation that the planet's atmosphere contains oxygen and that life is present
Photographs of the planet's surface that show clouds, oceans, and continents
Faster results, since each additional method halves the observing time for a system
A more complete picture of the planet's mass, radius, density, and orbit
quiz.e: Combining methods like transit and radial velocity yields more complete data (mass, radius, density, orbit) than either alone.

quiz.q: What was significant about the discovery of 51 Pegasi b's short orbital period?
o: It revealed that giant planets can orbit extremely close to their star ('hot Jupiters'), unlike anything in our solar system
It confirmed that most stars host Jupiter-like planets in wide, circular orbits, as in our solar system
It showed that planets orbiting pulsars are common, unlike those found around ordinary Sun-like stars
It demonstrated that exoplanets can be imaged directly, revealing giant planets in wide orbits around young stars
quiz.e: 51 Pegasi b orbits its star in just over 4 days, revealing the existence of 'hot Jupiters' with no solar system analog.

quiz.q: Why can microlensing events for exoplanet detection not be repeated or predicted?
o: Each event depends on a supernova near the host star, which happens once for any star
The planet orbits so quickly that its signal changes before follow-up observation is possible
Each event depends on a chance, one-time alignment of a foreground and background star
Light from the background star is blocked by the lens, so the same star cannot be observed again
quiz.e: Microlensing relies on a rare, unrepeatable alignment between a foreground star (with a planet) and a background star.

quiz.q: What did the discovery of exoplanets like hot Jupiters suggest about planet formation?
o: Planets form near their stars, then slowly drift outward over time
Planets form from stellar collisions, so close-in giants are leftover debris
Planets can migrate inward from where they originally formed
Planets keep their birth orbits, and stars have drifted toward them since
quiz.e: Hot Jupiters are thought to have formed farther from their star and migrated inward over time.

quiz.q: What is a limitation of using a single biosignature gas as evidence of life?
o: It must be measured by probes sent to the planet's surface, not by telescopes
It could result from non-biological chemical or geological processes instead
It fades from spectra too quickly to observe, since gases leave atmospheres fast
It cannot be distinguished from starlight, since stars produce the same gases
quiz.e: A single biosignature gas is not definitive since abiotic (non-biological) processes can sometimes produce similar signals.

quiz.q: What do transmission spectra reveal when starlight passes through a transiting planet's atmosphere?
o: The thickness of the planet's solid crust and its internal layers
The chemical composition of gases present in the atmosphere
The age of the host star and the date of the planet's formation
The planet's rotation speed and the tilt of its spin axis
quiz.e: Transmission spectroscopy identifies atmospheric gases by how they absorb specific wavelengths of the star's light.

quiz.q: What term describes an exoplanet not gravitationally bound to any star?
o: A rogue (or free-floating) planet
A hot Jupiter
A super-Earth
A circumbinary planet
quiz.e: Rogue planets drift through space unbound to any star and can be detected via gravitational microlensing.

quiz.q: Roughly how does a 'super-Earth' compare to Earth?
o: A planet smaller than Earth but larger than Mars, found orbiting Sun-like stars
It is a planet larger than Earth but smaller than Neptune-sized planets
A planet with Earth's size and mass but a hotter surface, found near red dwarfs
A planet larger than Neptune but smaller than Jupiter, with a thick gas envelope
quiz.e: Super-Earths are a size category between Earth and Neptune, a common type of exoplanet with no solar system counterpart.

quiz.q: What has JWST specifically enabled in exoplanet atmospheric studies?
o: Detecting molecules like water vapor and carbon dioxide in distant planetary atmospheres
Taking direct photographs of exoplanet surfaces, showing continents, oceans, and cloud patterns
Measuring the rotation periods of exoplanets by tracking surface features across their visible disks
Discovering the first exoplanets ever found, by watching stars wobble in visible light
quiz.e: JWST's sensitive infrared instruments have enabled detailed detection of atmospheric molecules on distant exoplanets.

quiz.q: Why is finding a planet in the habitable zone considered only a first step in the search for life?
o: The zone is defined by planet size, so it says little about orbital distance
Habitability also requires a suitable atmosphere and other planetary conditions
Planets in the zone are mostly gas giants, which have no surface where life could exist
Stars with habitable zones are very rare, so most searches must look in other galaxies
quiz.e: Orbital distance alone doesn't guarantee habitability; atmosphere, magnetic field, and geology also matter, as shown by Venus and Mars.

quiz.q: What do biosignatures ultimately provide in the search for extraterrestrial life?
o: Direct proof, since any detected biosignature gas must come from living organisms
Indirect evidence, not direct proof, of possible past or present life
Photographs of vegetation and animals on the planet's surface from space telescopes
A precise count of the number of species living on a distant planet
quiz.e: Biosignatures are indirect indicators requiring careful, cumulative evidence rather than single definitive proof.

flashcards.d: An imaginary sphere of arbitrarily large radius centered on Earth, used to map the apparent positions of stars and other sky objects.
The equatorial coordinate analogous to longitude, measured in hours (0-24) eastward from the vernal equinox.
The equatorial coordinate analogous to latitude, measuring angular distance north or south of the celestial equator.
A measure of how bright an object appears from Earth, on a logarithmic scale where lower/negative numbers mean brighter.
The brightness a star would have if placed at a standard distance of 10 parsecs from Earth, allowing true luminosity comparisons.
The time for Earth to rotate once relative to the distant stars, about 23 hours 56 minutes, shorter than the 24-hour solar day.
The Sun's apparent annual path across the celestial sphere, tilted 23.5 degrees to the celestial equator due to Earth's axial tilt.
Stars close enough to the celestial pole that, from a given latitude, they never set below the horizon.
The twinkling of stars caused by turbulent pockets of air in Earth's atmosphere refracting starlight.
A nine-level scale rating night-sky darkness from pristine (1) to inner-city light-polluted (9).
The roughly 23.5-degree tilt of Earth's rotation axis relative to its orbital plane, the true cause of the seasons.
The point in Earth's orbit (around June 21 or December 21) when a hemisphere is tilted most directly toward or away from the Sun.
The point in Earth's orbit (around March 20 or September 22) when neither hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun, giving near-equal day and night.
The 29.5-day cycle of lunar phases from new moon to new moon, as observed from Earth.
The Moon's 27.3-day orbital period measured relative to the fixed stars, shorter than the synodic month.
The dark, central part of a shadow where light is completely blocked; total eclipses occur only within an umbra.
A tide with the largest range, occurring at new and full moon when the Sun's and Moon's gravitational pulls align and combine.
A tide with the smallest range, occurring at quarter moons when the Sun's and Moon's tidal pulls partly cancel.
A state where an orbiting body's rotation period matches its orbital period, causing it to always show the same face — as the Moon does to Earth.
The roughly 11-year cycle of rising and falling solar magnetic activity, tracked by sunspot numbers.
A small, dense, rocky planet with a solid surface, such as Mercury, Venus, Earth, or Mars.
A large planet composed mainly of hydrogen and helium with no solid surface, such as Jupiter or Saturn.
A giant planet, like Uranus or Neptune, containing proportionally more water, ammonia, and methane ices than hydrogen/helium.
A process where a planet's atmosphere traps escalating amounts of heat, as on Venus, leading to extreme surface temperatures.
A region between Mars and Jupiter containing millions of rocky bodies left over from solar system formation.
A disk-shaped region beyond Neptune's orbit containing icy bodies, including Pluto, remnants of solar system formation.
A round body orbiting the Sun that has not cleared its orbital neighborhood of other debris, such as Pluto or Ceres.
The theory that the solar system formed from the gravitational collapse of a rotating cloud of gas and dust into a protoplanetary disk.
The glowing cloud of gas and dust surrounding a comet's nucleus, formed as solar heat vaporizes its ices near the Sun.
Internal heating of a moon caused by gravitational flexing from its parent planet, driving activity like Io's volcanism or Europa's ocean.
The full range of light wavelengths, from high-energy gamma rays to long-wavelength radio waves, of which visible light is a tiny slice.
A defect in refracting telescopes where a lens focuses different wavelengths of light at different points, causing color fringing.
The diameter of a telescope's primary lens or mirror, the key factor determining its light-gathering and resolving power.
A telescope's ability to distinguish fine detail or closely spaced objects, improved by larger aperture and shorter wavelength.
A technique combining signals from multiple telescopes to achieve the resolving power of a much larger single instrument.
A stretching of light to longer wavelengths, caused by an object moving away from the observer or by the expansion of space itself.
A shift of spectral lines to shorter wavelengths, indicating an object is moving toward the observer.
A spectrum with dark lines superimposed on a continuous background, produced when cooler gas absorbs specific wavelengths of light passing through it.
A technology that uses deformable mirrors adjusted in real time to counteract atmospheric turbulence, sharpening ground-based telescope images.
The practice of combining electromagnetic, gravitational-wave, and particle observations of the same cosmic event for a complete picture.
A collapsing cloud of gas and dust that has not yet ignited stable hydrogen fusion, the earliest stage of star formation.
The long, stable phase of a star's life spent fusing hydrogen into helium in its core; about 90% of stars, including the Sun, are here.
A plot of stellar temperature (or color) versus luminosity, used to classify stars by evolutionary stage.
An evolved star with an expanded, cooled outer envelope and a contracting, heating core, formed after core hydrogen exhaustion.
A glowing shell of gas expelled by a low- to medium-mass star near the end of its life, unrelated to planet formation despite the name.
The dense, Earth-sized remnant core left behind by a low- to medium-mass star, supported by electron degeneracy pressure.
The maximum mass (about 1.4 solar masses) a white dwarf can have before collapsing further into a neutron star.
An extremely dense stellar remnant, about 20 km across but more massive than the Sun, formed from the collapsed core of a massive star.
A rapidly rotating neutron star that emits beams of radiation appearing to pulse as they sweep past Earth.
A thermonuclear explosion of a white dwarf that has accreted enough mass from a companion star to exceed the Chandrasekhar limit; used as a standard candle in cosmology.
A flattened, rotating galaxy with a central bulge and spiral arms of gas, dust, and young stars, such as the Milky Way or Andromeda.
A smooth, roughly spherical or football-shaped galaxy of mostly old stars, with little gas, dust, or ongoing star formation.
The relationship v = H0 x d, stating that a galaxy's recession velocity is proportional to its distance, evidence that the universe is expanding.
The current rate of the universe's expansion, roughly 70 km/s per megaparsec, relating a galaxy's distance to its recession velocity.
An invisible form of matter, detected only through its gravitational effects, that makes up about 27% of the universe's mass-energy and explains galaxy rotation curves.
A mysterious repulsive property of space, making up about 68% of the universe's mass-energy, responsible for the accelerating expansion of the universe.
Faint microwave radiation left over from about 380,000 years after the Big Bang, considered strong evidence for the universe's hot, dense origin.
The scientific model that the universe began expanding from an extremely hot, dense state approximately 13.8 billion years ago.
The supermassive black hole, about 4 million solar masses, located at the center of the Milky Way galaxy.
The first artificial satellite, launched by the Soviet Union on October 4, 1957, which triggered the Space Race.
The 1969 NASA mission that achieved the first crewed Moon landing, with Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walking on the lunar surface.
The rocket used to launch the Apollo missions to the Moon; it remains the most powerful rocket ever successfully flown.
Twin NASA probes launched in 1977 that toured the outer planets; Voyager 1 is now the most distant human-made object, in interstellar space.
A NASA/ESA mission that orbited Saturn from 2004 to 2017 and landed the Huygens probe on the moon Titan in 2005.
A continuously crewed space station in low Earth orbit since 2000, built through international cooperation among the U.S., Russia, Europe, Japan, and Canada.
NASA's partially reusable crewed spacecraft, flown from 1981 to 2011, used to launch satellites and build the ISS.
The Soviet cosmonaut who became the first human in space, orbiting Earth aboard Vostok 1 on April 12, 1961.
NASA's current program aiming to return humans to the Moon as a step toward future crewed missions to Mars.
The NASA spacecraft that performed the first flyby of Pluto in 2015 and later explored a Kuiper Belt object in 2019.
An exoplanet detection technique that measures the periodic dimming of a star's light as a planet passes in front of it, revealing the planet's size.
An exoplanet detection technique that measures the Doppler shift caused by a star's gravitational wobble from an orbiting planet, revealing the planet's mass.
The range of orbital distances from a star where temperatures could allow liquid water to exist on a planet's surface; also called the 'Goldilocks zone'.
A measurable substance or pattern, such as atmospheric oxygen or methane, that provides indirect evidence of past or present life.
The first exoplanet confirmed orbiting a Sun-like star, discovered in 1995 via the radial velocity method; a 'hot Jupiter'.
A gas giant exoplanet that orbits extremely close to its host star, a planet type with no analog in our own solar system.
An exoplanet detection method that captures actual images of a planet by blocking a star's glare, generally limited to large, young, distant planets.
A detection method that finds exoplanets by the temporary magnification and distortion of a background star's light as a foreground star (with a planet) passes in front of it.
A planetary system with seven roughly Earth-sized planets orbiting a small red dwarf star, several within its habitable zone.
A probabilistic formula estimating the number of communicating civilizations in the galaxy based on factors like star formation rate and habitable planet fraction.

PART_A.q: What is the celestial sphere?
o: An imaginary sphere of arbitrarily large radius centered on Earth used to map apparent sky positions
The actual physical boundary of the solar system
A satellite tracking network
The plane of Earth's orbit
PART_A.e: The celestial sphere is a useful imaginary construct for mapping the apparent positions of stars without needing their true distances.

PART_A.q: Why does Earth experience seasons?
o: Because Earth's distance from the Sun changes dramatically
Because of Earth's 23.5-degree axial tilt
Because the Moon blocks sunlight part of the year
Because the Sun's brightness varies annually
PART_A.e: Seasons are caused by Earth's axial tilt, which changes how directly sunlight hits each hemisphere over the year; Earth is actually closest to the Sun in January.

PART_A.q: Why is Venus hotter than Mercury despite being farther from the Sun?
o: Venus has a faster rotation
Venus has a runaway greenhouse effect from its thick CO2 atmosphere
Venus is made of denser rock
Mercury has a reflective atmosphere
PART_A.e: Venus's thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat via the greenhouse effect, making its surface about 465C, hotter than Mercury despite Mercury's proximity to the Sun.

PART_A.q: Why are large modern telescopes almost always reflectors rather than refractors?
o: Mirrors are cheaper to manufacture than glass lenses
Large lenses sag under their own weight and refractors suffer chromatic aberration
Reflectors can be used only at night
Refractors cannot see visible light
PART_A.e: Large lenses are hard to support without sagging, and refracting telescopes suffer chromatic aberration; mirrors avoid this and can be built much larger.

PART_A.q: What determines a star's position on the main sequence of the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram?
o: Its distance from Earth
Its age since formation
Its mass, which sets temperature and luminosity
Its chemical composition of heavy elements only
PART_A.e: A star's mass primarily determines its temperature and luminosity, placing it at a particular point along the main sequence.

PART_A.q: What does Hubble's Law describe?
o: The rotation rate of the Milky Way
That a galaxy's recession velocity is proportional to its distance from us
The orbital period of planets
The temperature of the cosmic microwave background
PART_A.e: Hubble's Law (v = H0 x d) states that galaxies recede at speeds proportional to their distance, evidence that space itself is expanding.

PART_A.q: What event marked the start of the Space Race?
o: The launch of Sputnik 1 by the Soviet Union in 1957
The founding of NASA in 1958
Apollo 11's Moon landing in 1969
Yuri Gagarin's orbital flight in 1961
PART_A.e: The Soviet Union's launch of Sputnik 1 on October 4, 1957 triggered the Space Race and led directly to the creation of NASA in 1958.

PART_A.q: What does the transit method of exoplanet detection measure?
o: The star's gravitational wobble
The periodic dimming of a star's light as a planet passes in front of it
Direct photographs of the planet
Radio emissions from the planet's surface
PART_A.e: The transit method detects planets by the small, periodic dimming of a star's light when the planet passes between the star and Earth, revealing the planet's size.

PART_A.q: About how much brighter is a star of magnitude 1 compared to a star of magnitude 6?
o: 10 times
100 times
1,000 times
2.5 times
PART_A.e: Each 5-magnitude step corresponds to a brightness factor of 100, so a 5-magnitude difference (1 to 6) means the brighter star is about 100 times brighter.

PART_A.q: Why don't solar and lunar eclipses happen every month?
o: The Sun's distance from Earth varies too much
The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5 degrees relative to the ecliptic
The Moon is too small to cast a shadow most months
Earth's rotation prevents alignment
PART_A.e: Because the Moon's orbital plane is tilted about 5 degrees to the ecliptic, the Sun, Earth, and Moon are only aligned closely enough for an eclipse near the orbital nodes.

PART_A.q: Why was Pluto reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006?
o: It was found to be too small to be round
It has not cleared its orbital neighborhood of other Kuiper Belt objects
It does not orbit the Sun
It was found to be a moon of Neptune
PART_A.e: The IAU's 2006 definition requires a planet to have cleared its orbital neighborhood; Pluto shares its region with many other Kuiper Belt objects, so it was reclassified as a dwarf planet.

PART_A.q: What does redshift in a star's or galaxy's spectrum indicate?
o: The object is moving toward the observer
The object is moving away from the observer
The object is extremely hot
The object has a strong magnetic field
PART_A.e: Redshift is a shift of spectral lines to longer wavelengths, indicating that the object is moving away from the observer (or that space is expanding).

PART_A.q: What happens when a massive star's core turns to iron?
o: Fusion continues normally, releasing even more energy
Fusion can no longer support the core against gravity, leading to core collapse and a supernova
The star quietly cools into a white dwarf
The star begins fusing iron into heavier elements for billions of years
PART_A.e: Iron cannot be fused to release net energy; once a massive star's core turns to iron, fusion can no longer support it against gravity, triggering a core-collapse supernova.

PART_A.q: About what fraction of the universe's total mass-energy is dark energy estimated to be?
PART_A.e: Dark energy is estimated to make up about 68% of the universe's total mass-energy content, making it the dominant component overall.

PART_A.q: Which Apollo mission successfully landed the first humans on the Moon?
o: Apollo 8
Apollo 11
Apollo 13
Apollo 17
PART_A.e: Apollo 11 landed the first humans on the Moon on July 20, 1969, with Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walking on the surface.

PART_A.q: What does the radial velocity method of exoplanet detection primarily reveal about a planet?
o: Its exact radius
A lower limit on its mass, via the star's gravitational wobble
Its atmospheric composition
Its surface temperature directly
PART_A.e: Radial velocity detects the tiny periodic wobble of a star caused by an orbiting planet's gravity, revealing the planet's orbital period and a lower limit on its mass.

PART_A.q: What is the difference between a sidereal day and a solar day?
o: They are exactly the same length
A sidereal day is about 4 minutes shorter because Earth must rotate slightly more than 360 degrees for the Sun to return to the same spot
A solar day only occurs in summer
A sidereal day is measured relative to the Moon, not the stars
PART_A.e: Because Earth also moves along its orbit, it must rotate a bit more than 360 degrees for the Sun to return to the same position, making the solar day about 4 minutes longer than the sidereal day.

PART_A.q: What is the key difference between the synodic and sidereal months?
o: They are the same length, about 29.5 days
The synodic month (29.5 days) is the Moon's phase cycle; the sidereal month (27.3 days) is its true orbital period relative to the stars
The sidereal month is longer because it accounts for eclipses
The synodic month only applies during a full moon
PART_A.e: The synodic month (new moon to new moon, 29.5 days) is longer than the sidereal month (27.3 days) because Earth's own motion around the Sun changes the required geometry.

PART_A.q: Which body is thought to harbor a subsurface liquid water ocean beneath an icy crust, making it a top target in the search for life?
o: Mars
Europa
Mercury
Titan's atmosphere
PART_A.e: Jupiter's moon Europa is thought to have a subsurface liquid water ocean beneath its icy crust, making it a leading target in the search for extraterrestrial life.

PART_A.q: What is the main advantage of a larger telescope aperture?
o: It increases magnification most importantly
It increases both light-gathering power and angular resolution
It only affects the field of view
It eliminates the need for a mirror or lens
PART_A.e: Aperture size, not magnification, determines a telescope's light-gathering power (which scales with aperture squared) and its angular resolution.

PART_A.q: What is a Cepheid variable star used for in astronomy?
o: Measuring the temperature of the Sun's core
Serving as a 'standard candle' for measuring cosmic distances, since its pulsation period relates to its luminosity
Detecting gravitational waves
Determining a planet's atmospheric composition
PART_A.e: Cepheid variables pulsate in brightness with a period directly related to their true luminosity, making them useful standard candles for measuring distances to other galaxies.

PART_A.q: What is the Milky Way's central supermassive black hole called?
o: Sagittarius A*
Cygnus X-1
TON 618
PART_A.e: Sagittarius A*, located in the direction of the constellation Sagittarius, is the roughly 4-million-solar-mass supermassive black hole at the Milky Way's center.

PART_A.q: What was significant about the Voyager missions launched in 1977?
o: They were the first crewed missions beyond Earth orbit
They took advantage of a rare planetary alignment for a 'Grand Tour' of the outer planets
They were the first satellites to orbit Earth
They landed the first rovers on Mars
PART_A.e: Voyager 1 and 2 used a rare alignment of the outer planets to conduct a 'Grand Tour,' with Voyager 2 alone visiting Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune.

PART_A.q: What is the 'habitable zone' around a star?
o: The region where a planet's atmosphere is guaranteed to support life
The range of distances from a star where temperatures could allow liquid water on a planet's surface
The area closest to the star where planets form fastest
The zone where a star's magnetic field is strongest
PART_A.e: The habitable zone is the orbital distance range where surface temperatures could permit liquid water; being in this zone does not by itself guarantee habitability.

PART_A.q: What does apparent magnitude measure?
o: A star's true luminosity at a standard distance
How bright an object appears from Earth
The temperature of a star's surface
The distance to a star in light-years
PART_A.e: Apparent magnitude measures how bright an object looks from Earth, which depends on both its true luminosity and its distance from us.

PART_A.q: Why does the Moon contribute roughly twice the tidal effect of the Sun despite the Sun's far greater mass?
o: The Moon is made of denser material
Tidal force depends strongly on distance, and the Moon is much closer to Earth
The Sun's gravity does not affect tides at all
The Moon rotates faster than the Sun
PART_A.e: Tidal force falls off rapidly with distance, so despite being far less massive, the Moon's much closer distance gives it a stronger tidal influence than the Sun.

PART_A.q: What process explains how the solar system formed according to the nebular hypothesis?
o: A collision between two mature stars produced the planets
A rotating cloud of gas and dust collapsed under gravity into a flattened protoplanetary disk around the proto-Sun
Planets were captured one by one from interstellar space
The Sun formed after all the planets had already solidified
PART_A.e: The nebular hypothesis describes a rotating cloud of gas and dust collapsing under gravity and flattening into a protoplanetary disk, with planets forming from the leftover material.

PART_A.q: What did the Doppler effect on spectral lines most famously reveal about distant galaxies?
o: Their exact chemical composition only
Their recession velocities, leading to the discovery of the expanding universe
Their rotation rate only
Their surface gravity
PART_A.e: Doppler shifts in galaxy spectra revealed their recession velocities, a key piece of evidence that led to the discovery of the universe's expansion.

PART_A.q: What is the Chandrasekhar limit?
o: The maximum mass a white dwarf can have (about 1.4 solar masses) before collapsing further
The minimum mass needed to ignite hydrogen fusion
The maximum size a black hole's event horizon can reach
The boundary of the observable universe
PART_A.e: The Chandrasekhar limit, about 1.4 solar masses, is the maximum mass a white dwarf can support with electron degeneracy pressure before collapsing into a neutron star or triggering a Type Ia supernova.

PART_A.q: What is the significance of the cosmic microwave background (CMB)?
o: It is radiation from present-day star formation
It is leftover radiation from about 380,000 years after the Big Bang, strong evidence for the universe's hot, dense origin
It is radio noise from the Milky Way's core
It measures the current expansion rate of the universe directly
PART_A.e: The CMB, discovered accidentally in 1965, is radiation left over from about 380,000 years after the Big Bang and is one of the three main pillars of evidence for the Big Bang theory.

PART_B1.q: What causes a total lunar eclipse to often appear reddish, or a 'blood moon'?
o: The Moon's own surface minerals reflecting red light
Sunlight refracted through Earth's atmosphere reaching the Moon
The Moon passing through the asteroid belt
A reflection of Mars's light
PART_B1.e: During a total lunar eclipse, sunlight bent through Earth's atmosphere (mostly red wavelengths) illuminates the Moon, giving it a reddish 'blood moon' color.

PART_B1.q: What supports a white dwarf against further gravitational collapse?
o: Ongoing hydrogen fusion in its core
Electron degeneracy pressure
Its powerful magnetic field alone
Radiation pressure from helium fusion
PART_B1.e: White dwarfs no longer fuse elements; they are supported against collapse by electron degeneracy pressure, a quantum mechanical effect.

PART_B1.q: Why does the transit method miss many exoplanet systems?
o: It only works on stars smaller than the Sun
It requires the planet's orbit to be aligned edge-on as seen from Earth
It cannot detect planets larger than Jupiter
It only works for planets with atmospheres
PART_B1.e: The transit method depends on a fortunate edge-on orbital alignment so the planet passes in front of its star from our vantage point, so it misses systems without that alignment.

PART_B1.q: What is unusual about Uranus's axial tilt?
o: It has no measurable tilt at all
It is tilted about 98 degrees, essentially rotating on its side
It is tilted exactly like Earth's
Its tilt reverses every year
PART_B1.e: Uranus has an axial tilt of about 98 degrees, causing it to rotate essentially on its side, likely the result of an ancient massive collision.

PART_B1.q: What evidence led astronomers to conclude the universe's expansion is accelerating?
o: Rotation curves of nearby galaxies
Distant Type Ia supernovae in 1998 appearing dimmer (farther) than expected
The discovery of the cosmic microwave background
Direct imaging of dark energy particles
PART_B1.e: In 1998, observations showed distant Type Ia supernovae were dimmer, and thus farther away, than models predicted, revealing that the universe's expansion is accelerating.

PART_B1.q: Why do planets twinkle less than stars when viewed from Earth?
o: Planets are much farther away than stars
Planets present a small resolvable disk rather than a point source of light
Planets do not reflect any light
Planets are only visible during the day
PART_B1.e: Because planets show a small disk rather than a single point of light, atmospheric turbulence has less effect on them compared to the point-like light from distant stars.

PART_B1.q: Why do space telescopes like Hubble and JWST avoid using ground-based sites entirely?
o: To avoid atmospheric blurring and absorption of certain wavelengths
Because ground telescopes cannot use mirrors
Because launch costs are lower than construction costs
To eliminate the need for any calibration
PART_B1.e: Earth's atmosphere blurs images (seeing) and blocks most infrared, ultraviolet, and X-ray radiation, so space telescopes are needed to observe those wavelengths clearly.

PART_B1.q: What was the primary cause of the Apollo 13 mission's abort of its lunar landing?
o: A failed rocket launch
An oxygen tank explosion en route to the Moon
A collision with space debris
A software error in the guidance computer
PART_B1.e: An oxygen tank explosion during the flight to the Moon forced Apollo 13 to abort its planned lunar landing, and the crew's safe return became the mission's defining achievement.

PART_B1.q: What is the difference between spring tides and neap tides?
o: Spring tides only occur in spring season; neap tides occur in other seasons
Spring tides occur at new and full moon when Sun and Moon align, producing a larger tidal range; neap tides occur at quarter moons when the pulls partly cancel
Neap tides are always larger than spring tides
Spring tides are caused only by the Sun
PART_B1.e: Spring tides (larger range) occur when the Sun and Moon align at new and full moon; neap tides (smaller range) occur at quarter moons when solar and lunar tidal forces partly cancel.

PART_B1.q: What triggers a Type Ia supernova?
o: A single massive star simply running out of hydrogen fuel
A white dwarf in a binary system accreting enough matter from a companion to exceed the Chandrasekhar limit
Two neutron stars colliding directly
A star's core suddenly turning into pure iron
PART_B1.e: A Type Ia supernova occurs when a white dwarf accretes matter from a companion star until it exceeds the Chandrasekhar limit, triggering a runaway thermonuclear explosion.

PART_B1.q: What is a key limitation of gravitational microlensing for exoplanet detection?
o: It can only detect planets orbiting the Sun
Each microlensing event is unrepeatable and unpredictable
It cannot detect free-floating rogue planets
It only works for gas giant planets
PART_B1.e: Microlensing events depend on a chance alignment of a foreground and background star and cannot be repeated or predicted, unlike transit or radial velocity monitoring.

PART_B1.q: What is the source of most of the solar system's short-period comets and Near-Earth objects reservoirs?
o: The asteroid belt only
The Kuiper Belt and the more distant Oort Cloud
The rings of Saturn
The core of the Sun
PART_B1.e: The Kuiper Belt, beyond Neptune, and the distant Oort Cloud are reservoirs of icy bodies believed to supply many of the solar system's comets.

PART_B1.q: What do galaxy rotation curves reveal that led to the concept of dark matter?
o: Stars near a galaxy's center orbit faster than visible mass can explain
Stars far from a galaxy's center orbit faster than visible matter alone can explain
All stars in a galaxy orbit at exactly the same speed
Galaxies do not rotate at all
PART_B1.e: Stars far from a galaxy's visible center orbit faster than expected from visible mass alone, implying large amounts of unseen mass, or dark matter, extending well beyond the visible disk.

PART_B1.q: What is the ecliptic?
o: The boundary of the Milky Way galaxy
The Sun's apparent annual path against the background stars
The Moon's orbital plane around Earth
The line marking Earth's equator
PART_B1.e: The ecliptic is the Sun's apparent yearly path through the background stars, tilted about 23.5 degrees relative to the celestial equator.

PART_B1.q: What does a continuous spectrum, without absorption or emission lines, typically indicate about its source?
o: A cool, diffuse gas cloud
A hot, dense object, such as a star's interior
A supermassive black hole's event horizon
An object with no temperature at all
PART_B1.e: A continuous spectrum is produced by hot, dense objects like the interior of a star, in contrast to the absorption or emission lines produced by cooler or hotter, less dense gas.

PART_B1.q: What is the International Space Station's approximate orbital period around Earth?
o: About 24 hours
About 90 minutes
About 1 week
About 27 days
PART_B1.e: The ISS orbits Earth at about 400 km altitude, completing one orbit roughly every 90 minutes, or about 16 orbits per day.

PART_B1.q: What phenomenon is responsible for the Moon always showing the same face to Earth?
o: The Moon does not rotate at all
Tidal locking, or synchronous rotation, matching the Moon's rotation period to its orbital period
Earth's magnetic field holding the Moon in place
The Moon's orbit being perfectly circular
PART_B1.e: The Moon is tidally locked to Earth, meaning its rotation period exactly matches its orbital period, so the same face always points toward Earth.

PART_B1.q: What eventually happens to the outer layers of a Sun-like star as it becomes a red giant and then dies?
o: They are ejected, forming a glowing planetary nebula around the exposed white dwarf core
They collapse into a neutron star
They are blown away in a core-collapse supernova
They remain fused together as a black hole forms
PART_B1.e: Low- to medium-mass stars expel their outer layers as a planetary nebula, leaving behind the hot, exposed core, which becomes a white dwarf.

PART_B1.q: What did the 1995 discovery of 51 Pegasi b demonstrate?
o: The first confirmed exoplanet around a Sun-like star, detected via radial velocity
The first exoplanet imaged directly with a telescope
The first Earth-sized planet in a habitable zone
The first planet detected by transit photometry
PART_B1.e: 51 Pegasi b, discovered in 1995 by Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz using radial velocity, was the first confirmed exoplanet found orbiting a Sun-like star.

PART_B1.q: What are the four 'terrestrial' planets in our solar system?
o: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune
Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars
Earth, Mars, Ceres, Pluto
Mercury, Earth, Jupiter, Neptune
PART_B1.e: Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars are the terrestrial planets: small, rocky worlds with solid surfaces, as opposed to the gas and ice giants further out.

PART_B2.q: Why does a comet's tail always point away from the Sun regardless of its direction of travel?
o: Gravity pulls the tail away from the Sun
Solar wind and radiation pressure push the tail away from the Sun
The tail is an optical illusion caused by Earth's atmosphere
Comets always travel away from the Sun
PART_B2.e: A comet's tail is shaped by solar wind and radiation pressure pushing gas and dust away from the Sun, so the tail always points outward regardless of the comet's motion.

PART_B2.q: What is a major challenge in interpreting a potential biosignature gas like oxygen in an exoplanet's atmosphere?
o: Oxygen cannot be detected by any current instrument
Some biosignature gases can also be produced by non-biological geological or photochemical processes
Oxygen only exists on planets with confirmed life
Telescopes cannot measure atmospheric gases at all
PART_B2.e: False positives are a major challenge because some candidate biosignature gases, including oxygen, can be produced abiotically, so strong claims of life require multiple corroborating lines of evidence.

PART_B2.q: Why do more massive stars have much shorter lifespans than less massive stars, despite having more hydrogen fuel?
o: They convert mass to energy less efficiently
They burn through fuel far faster due to much higher core temperatures and fusion rates
They contain less hydrogen relative to their size
They do not undergo fusion at all
PART_B2.e: More massive stars have hotter, denser cores that fuse hydrogen far more rapidly, so despite having more fuel, they exhaust it much faster and live far shorter lives.

PART_B2.q: Why is Earth closest to the Sun in January even though it is winter in the Northern Hemisphere?
o: Earth's orbital distance from the Sun does not cause the seasons; axial tilt does
January is actually summer everywhere on Earth
The Sun's energy output is lowest in January
Earth's orbit is a perfect circle so distance never changes
PART_B2.e: Seasons are governed by Earth's 23.5-degree axial tilt, not by orbital distance; Earth reaches perihelion (closest to the Sun) in early January during Northern Hemisphere winter.

PART_B2.q: What made the Space Shuttle only partially reusable rather than fully reusable?
o: The orbiter was discarded after every flight
The large external fuel tank was discarded on every flight, while the orbiter and boosters were recovered and reused
None of its components were ever reused
The solid rocket boosters burned up completely each launch
PART_B2.e: The Space Shuttle's orbiter and solid rocket boosters were recovered and reused, but its large external fuel tank was discarded and not reused on every flight.

PART_B2.q: Why is interferometry, as used by the Event Horizon Telescope, valuable in astronomy?
o: It combines signals from multiple telescopes to achieve the resolving power of a much larger single telescope
It eliminates the need for any telescope aperture at all
It only works for radio wavelengths and no others
It increases a telescope's magnification without changing resolution
PART_B2.e: Interferometry combines signals from an array of telescopes so their combined resolving power matches that of a single telescope as wide as the array's total span.

PART_B2.q: What is the difference between the horizontal (alt-azimuth) and equatorial coordinate systems?
o: They are identical and interchangeable
The horizontal system depends on the observer's location and time, while the equatorial system is fixed to the stars
The equatorial system only works in the Southern Hemisphere
The horizontal system uses right ascension and declination
PART_B2.e: The alt-azimuth system is specific to an observer's location and time (altitude and azimuth), while the equatorial system (right ascension, declination) is fixed to the celestial sphere regardless of observer position.

PART_B2.q: What distinguishes an elliptical galaxy from a spiral galaxy?
o: Elliptical galaxies have prominent spiral arms and active star formation
Elliptical galaxies are smooth, roughly spherical collections of older stars with little gas or new star formation
Spiral galaxies have no central bulge
Elliptical galaxies always contain a bar of stars through the center
PART_B2.e: Elliptical galaxies are smooth, roughly spherical or football-shaped systems dominated by older stars, with little gas, dust, or ongoing star formation, unlike star-forming spiral galaxies.

PART_B2.q: What is the primary composition difference between the asteroid belt's largest member, Ceres, and typical Kuiper Belt objects?
o: Ceres is a rocky dwarf planet in the inner asteroid belt, while Kuiper Belt objects are icy bodies far beyond Neptune
Ceres is made entirely of ice, like Kuiper Belt objects
Kuiper Belt objects are hotter than Ceres
There is no meaningful difference between them
PART_B2.e: Ceres, the largest asteroid, is a rocky dwarf planet located between Mars and Jupiter, while Kuiper Belt objects are icy bodies located in the outer solar system beyond Neptune.

PART_B2.q: What advantage does combining radial velocity data with transit data give astronomers studying an exoplanet?
o: It reveals the planet's density, allowing them to infer whether it is rocky, gaseous, or icy
It eliminates the need to know the planet's orbital period
It only works for planets outside the habitable zone
It reveals the planet's exact surface temperature with no other data needed
PART_B2.e: Radial velocity gives a planet's mass and transit data gives its radius; combining the two lets astronomers calculate density and infer whether the planet is rocky, gaseous, or icy.

PART_C.q: Written response: choose TWO concepts from different units and construct an argument connecting them. Cite specific evidence from each.
o: Names both concepts precisely, gives concrete evidence for each, and explains the causal/logical bridge
Lists the two topics without connecting them
Describes only one concept in detail
Gives a personal opinion with no course evidence
PART_C.e: Strong responses anchor every claim in specific unit content.

PART_C.q: Essay plan: identify the single most important takeaway of this course. Defend it using three units as evidence, then address one counterargument.
o: Clear thesis, three unit-specific pieces of evidence, genuine counterargument, resolution
Thesis with no support
Topic list with no argument
Anecdote unrelated to course content
PART_C.e: Full argumentative architecture earns top marks.

workedExamples.title: Wavelength and color
workedExamples.prompt: A star appears blue. What does that suggest about its surface temperature?
steps: Hot objects emit light at shorter wavelengths.
Blue light has a shorter wavelength than red light.
So a blue star is hotter than a red one.
workedExamples.answer: The star has a high surface temperature.
